transcript.text: My Dyson V10 Absolute (SV12) won't run at all now. On the battery display there's a red light flashing when I press the trigger, then nothing. It was charging overnight. Do I need a new battery or is the whole thing dead?

A flashing red battery light on a Dyson V10 when the trigger is pressed usually indicates a battery fault, rather than a blocked cleaner head or a dead motor. The machine is seeing the trigger command but the battery protection circuitry is refusing to supply power.

It does not automatically mean the whole vacuum is dead. The battery is the most likely failed part, especially if it was left charging overnight but still gives the same red flash.

Before buying anything, try these quick checks:

1. Use a different wall socket and plug the Dyson charger directly into it (not an extension lead).
2. Inspect and reseat the charger and battery connections. Unplug the charger first. If your V10 has a removable battery, remove it and refit it firmly.
3. Check for dirt or moisture on the contacts where the battery meets the handle. Wipe with a dry lint-free cloth only.
4. Remove/clean the filter and check the airway for blockages. A blockage normally causes pulsing/cutting out rather than an immediate red battery warning, but it is worth ruling out. Ensure a washed filter has dried for at least 24 hours before refitting.
5. Charge it again for about 3.5 hours. A normal charge should show blue lights; a repeated red flash is not normal.

If it still flashes red immediately every time you press the trigger, the practical next step is usually a replacement V10/SV12 battery. Get one specifically listed as compatible with your particular SV12 version and battery fitting style; there are screw-in and click-in versions, and battery variants are not all interchangeable. A genuine Dyson battery is the safest choice.

Do not keep charging or using it if the battery is swollen, unusually hot, damaged, smells odd, or has leaked—replace it and arrange proper battery recycling.

If the vacuum is still within Dyson’s warranty, contact Dyson before purchasing a battery. They can confirm the flash code and may replace the battery or diagnose the charger/machine. But based on your description, battery failure is much more likely than the entire machine having failed.

I've tried the hallway socket as well, and charged it for 3.5 hours with the charger plugged straight into the battery. Blue lights come on while charging, but it still flashes red when I press the trigger. The filter was washed last month and nothing is blocked, the contacts look clean, and the battery is screwed in so it doesn't wiggle. It isn't swollen, hot or smelly. It's about 4.5 years old, so the 2-year guarantee has run out. I'd rather not unscrew anything before I've spoken to Dyson about cost.

Given those checks, a failed battery is now the most likely cause.

The blue lights while charging show that the charger is delivering power and the battery is at least accepting a charge indication. But a red flash as soon as the trigger is pulled usually means the battery’s internal protection/management circuit detects a fault or cannot supply current under load. At around 4½ years old, that is a plausible end-of-life battery failure.

You do not need to unscrew or dismantle anything before contacting Dyson. In fact, your next sensible step is to ask them for a diagnosis/price first. Have ready:

• Model: Dyson V10 Absolute / SV12
• The machine serial number (normally on the main body/handle area)
• Symptom: charges with blue lights, but flashes red immediately on trigger and will not run
• Checks already completed: alternate socket, direct charging, clean contacts, no blockage, dry/clean filter, battery physically secure, no swelling/heat/damage.

Ask them specifically whether they regard the red flash as a battery fault code, and what the price and availability are for the correct screw-in replacement battery. They may also be able to tell you whether your serial number takes a particular battery revision.

Unless Dyson identifies something unusual, this is much more likely to need a battery than a complete replacement vacuum. Keep it unplugged when not actively checking it, and don’t continue repeated trigger/charge attempts if the red fault continues.
